papers.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
papers.abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

papers.title: A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
papers.abstract: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade -- the model for rumour and adoption spread on social networks -- embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd (density-dependent blocking), so the swarm aggregates on a resource, then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and physical space are one coupled system, and this feedback -- not tuning -- makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a matter of percolation, and past a critical connectivity the swarm holds itself in a cascade window -- locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, sandpile-like drive-avalanche cycle. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours foraging biology documents separately emerge together -- recruitment, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These are not coincidences but one least-committal principle: the resource field and the search both follow from maximum entropy -- Levy search matched to the field's sparsity, recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging are one system in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. Percolating cascades yield a large return on minimal communication. And that sparse, clustered field is the generic one -- resources almost inevitably aggregate, and maximum entropy makes it the least-committal one once they do -- so one untuned rule should recur widely.

papers.title: Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly connected through networks and take on tasks that require negotiation and joint decision-making, a systematic approach is needed to assess how their views converge and what information supports their decisions. We present an evaluation framework that treats consensus formation as the evolution of publicly stated positions toward a shared region, using accumulated communication history as context. The framework tracks position trajectories, group dispersion, and information expressed in public messages. Two case studies examine staffing decisions based on distributed facts and decisions requiring agents to reconcile duplicate information and a cancelled contract. Results from 1,872 completed runs associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, while the second task reveals persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers. Membership-change experiments provide a complementary evaluation. By separating convergence among agents from progress toward a task's full-information answer, the framework relates decision accuracy and bounded disagreement to the information available during the exchange.

papers.title: Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
papers.abstract: A principal designs ratings for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talents, mapping outputs into arbitrary finite-variance statistics. Peer output both benchmarks effort and signals talent, making full disclosure suboptimal under confidential ratings. Relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality yields a closed-form rating and computable effort bounds for general priors; under normality, the relaxation is exact. Optimal confidential ratings combine the full-disclosure wage with the Fisher score for effort: they are relative-performance when individual output is informative about talent and team-based when it is noisy. Public ratings must satisfy joint Bayes plausibility, weakening incentives; hence, the principal prefers confidential ratings, whereas agents prefer public ratings. A spectral decomposition characterizes public ratings under normality: small cost heterogeneity implies full disclosure regardless of the noise structure, whereas large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers can induce partial disclosure to reallocate incentives. The results bear on performance ratings and pay transparency.

Shows confidential ratings combine full-disclosure wages with Fisher-score-based incentives, shifting between relative-performance and team-based ratings depending on informativeness. Characterizes when public ratings require full versus partial disclosure based on cost heterogeneity and effort spillovers.

papers.title: No-Regret Revenue Maximization in Sequential Market Making Under Inventory Constraints
papers.abstract: Market makers keep trading efficient by setting bid and ask prices for buyers and sellers. In sequential market making, trades happen independently based on price thresholds, requiring the market maker to maintain balanced, low-risk inventory over T rounds. This paper studies how to maximize revenue with unknown buyer and seller valuations using regret minimization. When the market maker only sees trade success or failure, an algorithm achieves regret and inventory bounds proportional to T to the power of 2/3. When full order book data is available for failed trades, regret and inventory limits improve significantly to the square root of T. We also establish a fundamental trade-off via a lower bound, by proving that tighter round-by-round inventory limits strictly force higher minimum regret.

papers.one_sentence: Studies regret-minimizing algorithms for a market maker setting bid/ask prices under unknown valuations and inventory constraints over T rounds. Shows regret and inventory bounds scale as T^(2/3) with binary trade feedback, improving to square-root-T with full order book data. Proves a lower bound showing tighter inventory limits force higher minimum regret.
